title: Are we developing games or just building features?
author: hezakidenzel
selftext:
Hey everyone! I'm new to game development and currently working on a space game called Star Take.

One of the biggest challenges I've faced, and something I've seen other developers struggle with, is making my own game fun. After all, if I don't enjoy playing it, why would anyone else?

Initially, I focused on multiplayer and building countless mechanics. I decided to reverse that process, focusing on the offline experience first and making the existing mechanics genuinely fun.

Now, I spend more time playing my own game, identifying improvements, and balancing enemies rather than adding features simply because they sound cool.

This change made me genuinely enjoy playing my own game.

Has anyone else experienced something similar during development?

comments.author: count023
comments.body: aren't games just a pile of features onto a previous game you wanted and never got? Expedition 33 was, "what if we added Sekiro features to Final Fantasy 7". GTA6 was "what if we added cars to red dead redemption"? Wasn't Quake just "what if Doom set in castles in 3d?"

replies.author: hydroxyHU
replies.body: I think there's a difference between having a lot of features and making a good game. You can throw together twenty cool mechanics, but that doesn't mean they'll create an enjoyable experience. It's more about how they work together, the pacing, and whether they actually serve the gameplay. Sometimes five well-connected features are worth more than twenty disconnected ones.

replies.author: JinAnkabut
replies.body:
This oversimplification seems worryingly popular in this sub. I definitely got more out of E33 than just ff7xSekiro.

Game devs do more than mash features together. Designing an experience that holds your attention for hours is skill that goes beyond what you've described.

replies.author: count023
replies.body: but at the same time, designing the experience is literally bringing together features to see how they play, and usually a game dev is taking inspiration from things that have come before, not inventing in a void.

replies.body:
I'm frankly unsure which features made me care about the narrative, which spurred me to give it so much attention. I'd argue that the combat, while great, was the least interesting part to me. 

If you argue that story telling is a feature, fine, but I think it's a bad faith argument.

comments.author: hydroxyHU
comments.body:
I can definitely relate to this.

I'm currently developing a manga artist career sim, and I recently caught myself falling into the same trap: adding more genres, research options, systems and little features because they seemed like good ideas.

But after spending several hours actually playing through my own game, I realized that adding more content doesn't automatically make the experience better. In fact, one of my recent updates introduced so many new research options that it disrupted a progression rhythm that had previously felt pretty good.

So I went back, adjusted how content is unlocked, and started focusing much more on pacing and how the existing systems work together.

I think there's a big difference between having a lot of things the player *can do* and giving them reasons to *want to do them*.

I've started treating playtesting as part of development, not just something you do when development is almost finished. Sometimes the best update is removing friction or fixing the pacing rather than adding another feature.

And honestly, I've been enjoying playing my own game a lot more since I started doing that.

replies.author: hezakidenzel
replies.body: It’s good to know that; we are heading in the right direction.

comments.author: fairerman
comments.body:
Few things about that.
First, we usually think a lot of mechanics and what we want in the game, however, I could say that those are the "big shapes". Like, when we think about that, our feeling are abstract about what we want. In our mind, we imagine the fun, but we don't know exactly how to put it into practice. Something I've thought recently about that is, take a game that you like and inspired you and make notes about what you think it's fun on it and which feelings you get from it. I wanna make a action game and one of the games that I'll "study" is Sengoku Basara, I'm having fun while playing it, why? Even if the game is so repetitive, why is it fun? The characters look cool and unique, the route is always simple, your character is way stronger than enemies, the sounds effects are cool and immersive. It's a game where you don't have to think too much and go kill bunch of enemies. I also enjoy a lot AC Odyssey and I'll do the same on that game.

replies.author: hezakidenzel
replies.body: That's a really good point! I like your approach of studying not just the mechanics of other games, but also the feelings they create. Sometimes we focus so much on what a game should have that we forget why people actually enjoy playing it. Thanks for sharing your perspective!

comments.body:

bla bla bla.  
  
engagement question?"

replies.author: hezakidenzel
replies.body: I understand why it might come across that way, but my intention was genuinely to discuss the challenges of making a game fun. I mentioned my game simply to provide context about my personal experience. The discussion itself is more important to me than promoting the game.

comments.author: DisasterNarrow4949
comments.body:
This is the difference of producing AI Slop and an actual game. 

For me, I didn't experienced it because I genuinelly love game design and designing games so I just cannot simply keep adding features without playtesting, balancing, brainstorming etc., because that is the whole deal of game deving for me. 

That is why I love vibe coding my games. Now I'm basically able to work fully as a game designer, which is what I love, even being a single garage developer.

replies.author: hezakidenzel
replies.body: We should be more like you; I have plenty of ideas, but lack organization—much like most "vibecoding" creators.

replies.author: Salientsnake4
replies.body: This is how game dev should work in practice anyways. You scope out and design the MVP, which should be designed in a way that it'd be fun. Then you build it, and playtest looking for bugs and features to improve the experiment. You iterate until its polished and very fun, and then you find playtesters and take their feedback and iterate and add new features.

comments.author: Brettinabox
comments.body: If you keep the mindset of forcing your self to have fun, project will likely never be finished.

replies.author: hezakidenzel
replies.body: I don't think so; I'm actually having quite a lot of fun with the game right now.

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body: I hope so, im making my own and hopefully the 100s of testing runs doesnt burn me out.

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
It is natural to reach this stage. At some point you realize that your first idea is just X game with the mechanics you want. That is fine in it self, but yes, probably means you will be over shadowed by the game you are inspired by. Eventually you learn the tricks, like how games need an hook and anchors. The reverse is when you learn that original doesn't mean better.

Game development isn't an small thing, you will have many epiphanies.

replies.author: hezakidenzel
replies.body: It’s good to know that; we are heading in the right direction.

comments.author: IndiBestEngineer
comments.body: same lesson here. what helped me was measuring instead of guessing: posthog on one of my browser games showed a median of 5 lives and 12 minutes per session. if the median player never reaches a feature, it doesn't exist for them.

comments.author: Salientsnake4
comments.body:
I've seen this whole "it's hard to make my game fun" compaint a few times now. I'm making games that I'd want to play and naturally thats fun for me. Each of the games I develop I put dozens of hours or more into just playing for fun, not counting the playtesting or balancing hours I've put in. 

That's just my perspective, not a knock on anyone.

comments.author: Kindly-Sail6260
comments.body:
You’re just describing what happens when trad developers make their games. They usually start with core mechanics before adding in features. But you’re doing the opposite of reversing all your features to work on a single mechanic. Going forward you should start with one system at a time. 

AI just gives you that feeling that you can inject all the features because features are what make a game fun. What makes a game fun is the core mechanic first. Features are the cherry on top. 

Hope this helps. Keep building!
